title: T cell responses after yellow fever and other vaccinations
summary: T cells and B cells are cells of the immune system and as such are centrally involved in the defense against infections. In principle, they can be found throughout the body, but are consistently present in the blood. Vaccinations are carried out with parts of the pathogen against which the vaccination is to be carried out. These parts of the pathogen (so-called antigens) then trigger an immune response. The triggering of a T and B cell response is one of the most important quality features of vaccinations. In contrast to the B-cell-based immune response, the T-cell immune response following vaccination is still incompletely understood. The aim of the scientific study is to characterize the human T cell response after vaccination (e.g. yellow fever vaccination with YFV-17D vaccine) in more detail. For this purpose, we will examine T cells that are directed against yellow fever or another vaccine antigen using molecular biology. We will also determine tissue compatibility antigens (HLA molecules). HLA molecules are used, among other things, to bind vaccine antigens, which are then recognized by T cells.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Vaccination with the vaccine for which the immune responses is to be investigated
Exclusion criteria:
a) Incapable of giving consent 
b) Minors 
c) Pregnant or breastfeeding women 
d) Persons who are in a dependent relationship with other study participants or the study investigators
